title: The repair is only half the job
text: A customer leaves a broken mixer at a repair shop. The technician can diagnose it, but the work soon spreads across handwritten notes, parts enquiries, estimate approvals, and pickup reminders. Each interruption steals time from the repair bench. Benchbook is built for small repair shops that need a clear path from intake to pickup. It organizes the coordination around the technician, while keeping diagnosis, approval, and quality control in human hands.

title: A clear workbench from the first intake
text: This is the live Benchbook application, running on public cloud hosting with PostgreSQL persistence. The demo uses synthetic customer details and a sample parts catalogue. We load repair jobs for familiar Tamil Nadu appliances and open one ticket. The timeline makes the current stage visible, alongside the complaint and technician notes. A refresh keeps the job because the record lives in the database. The evaluator does not need my computer to stay online.

title: Useful advice with traceable context
text: The technician records what was actually observed. Then we request parts advice. A real Strands agent reads bounded job and catalogue context and returns a suggestion with visible provenance. In our live verification, the response included an observed tool call and a catalogue reference. The catalogue is a demonstration resource, not a promise of supplier stock or current market prices. The technician still checks compatibility and decides what belongs in the estimate. The assistant never silently orders a part.

title: Approval is a visible step
text: Next comes the estimate and customer approval stage. Benchbook keeps that decision separate from an assistant suggestion. The workflow requires the appropriate human confirmation before moving ahead. These public demo roles demonstrate a boundary; they are not a production identity verification system. We can inspect the stage history to understand what changed. Version checks help reject stale changes, and retries preserve the operation identity. This makes coordination clearer without pretending that automation has replaced the technician's responsibility.

title: From repair work to a ready pickup
text: Once the approved work proceeds, the ticket continues through its repair and quality-control stages. The technician confirms completion and checks the result before the job can move to pickup. A customer update is prepared as a draft for a human to review. Benchbook does not send a real message in this demonstration. Closing the job records the outcome and keeps the history available. The point is a dependable sequence, so a repaired appliance is not forgotten while the shop moves to its next customer.

title: Persistent workflow. Bounded assistant.
text: The React interface talks to a FastAPI service on Vercel, backed by Neon PostgreSQL. The Strands assistant uses Groq with bounded requests, admission limits, and explicit failure states. Workflow rules are enforced in the service rather than only by disabled buttons. Human confirmation is separate from advisory output. The public release was checked for database readiness, persistent workflow behavior, and real model execution. Free service limits still apply; an unavailable assistant must be reported honestly rather than replaced by fabricated advice.

title: Less chasing. More repair.
text: Benchbook is for a technician who wants to spend more time repairing and less time reconstructing the status of every job. Its value is visible next steps, reviewable suggestions, and a history that survives the browser. The current release demonstrates the complete coordination workflow with synthetic data. Stronger shop identity and verified supplier integrations are future work. Today, the live demo and public source let judges inspect both the working product and its limits.
